query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The evolution of a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is driven by the formation of stable intermetallic compounds, which in turn changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior.
generation.mechanism: Formation of stable intermetallic compounds through thermal treatment or mechanical alloying, leading to changes in corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of intermetallic compound formation and its effect on corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior is not fully understood

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled comparison of as-cast and thermally treated alloys in corrosive environments
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated alloy shows no improvement in corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: One promising design strategy involves the development of multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), which incorporate multiple elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios to achieve property combinations beyond those achievable in conventional binary or ternary systems. While this concept has been widely explored in high-entropy alloys, its application to Mg-rich systems remains limited and may offer new pathways for improving corrosion resistance, mechanical performance, and maintaining a low density. While prior studies have investigated Mg-Ti, Mg-Zn, and Zn-Ti binary alloys individually, the combined effects of Ti and Zn in bulk Mg-rich multi-element systems remain poorly understood, particularly with respect to phase stability, passivation behavior, and mechanical properties.

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. AbstractIn as-cast (AC) or heat-treated (HT) metallic ultra-high temperature materials often “conventional” and complex-concentrated (CC) or high-entropy (HE) solid solutions (sss) are observed. Refractory metal containing bcc sss also are contaminated with oxygen. This paper studied the stability of CC/HE Nbss and the contamination with oxygen of Nbss in RM(INb)ICs, RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs and RM(Nb)ICs/RHEAs. “Conventional” and CC/HE Nbss were compared. “Conventional” Nbss can be Ti-rich only in AC alloys. Ti-rich Nbss is not observed in HT alloys. In B containing alloys the Ti-rich Nbss is usually CC/HE. The CC/HE Nbss is stable in HT alloys with simultaneous addition of Mo, W with Hf, Ge+Sn. The implications for alloy design of correlations between the parameter δ of “conventional” and CC/HE Nbss with the B or the Ge+Sn concentration in the Nbss and of relationships of other solutes with the B or Ge+Sn content are discussed. The CC/HE Nbss has low Δχ, VEC and Ω and high ΔSmix, |ΔHmix| and δ parameters, and is formed in alloys that have high entropy of mixing.
